rss.summary: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026". They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same). The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5. Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others. Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58). rss.title: Rapidly scaling online storage to serve over 1 billion ChatGPT users (Part II)
rss.summary: Learn how OpenAI scaled Habitat with reliable multi-tenancy, global caching, and Azure Cosmos DB to deliver 12× faster reads for ChatGPT.
rss.text_excerpt:
All OpenAI products require fast, reliable access to data, provided by our storage platform, Habitat. It has to respond in milliseconds to over 1 billion users across 40 geographic regions. Our infrastructure faced an extraordinary challenge: supporting explosive growth and new use cases while continuing to improve reliability, performance, and product developer velocity. Solving that challenge required rethinking how our online storage platform was designed and operated. We constantly evaluated tradeoffs, following the pattern of: first become reliable enough for mission-critical product traffic, then fast enough for global users, and, finally, to deftly operate at massive scale. This two-part series explains how we developed Habitat from a simple client library and database into a globally distributed storage platform serving over 500 petabytes of data. Part I focused on Habitat’s evolution from a Python client to a service. It also covered the techniques that allowed us to push a Python-based service far beyond what many would consider practical. In this post, Part II, we walk through how we scaled the underlying storage component: Azure Cosmos DB. Through a close working partnership with the Azure team, we arrived at a viable multi-tenancy approach of co-managed containers, with excellent read performance at massive, global scale. Request Response Changes (CDC) As companies scale, infra teams often evolve from running single-tenant systems to multi-tenant ones. Single-tenancy, where every product surface team maintains their own system, reduces blast radius and provides easy ownership boundaries and workload isolation. As teams and product surfaces grow, this becomes expensive to run. Single-tenancy makes every product team responsible for capacity planning and often results in significant over-provisioning. Conversely, multi-tenancy assigns control to a centralized database team, with better knowledge and experience for provisioning resources. But multi-tenancy creates its own problems, such as noisy-neighbor issues, where one tenant consumes an unusually large share of the resources to the detriment of the other tenants. In Habitat, we had to weigh all these tradeoffs to design a reliable, efficient, storage system at scale. rss.title: AI Is Getting Good at Math. Here’s Why.
rss.summary: AI models are solving more mathematical problems. A pattern is emerging in their successes that could help us predict which problems they’ll solve next.
rss.text_excerpt:
The question that interests me is whether we can predict what kinds of problems these models will solve. What makes a problem tractable for an LLM, and what do these solutions have in common? If AI solves problems differently from humans, identifying the difference should help us decide where to point it. The unit-distance disproof has the richest commentary, so let’s start there. Problem complexity Here is a simple mental model. To solve any given problem, you need a sequence of hints or insights with work between them. This maps surprisingly well to simple everyday problems and to complex ideas like General Relativity (see Bonus). The sequence looks something like this: Insight -> time / effort -> insight -> time/effort -> solution. An expert would need fewer hints than a beginner would, as they would have more background. In his commentary on unit-distance proof, WT Gowers uses a similar idea: the difficulty of the proof is the shortest sequence of hints that would let experts reconstruct it. He calls it Kolmogorov complexity modulo experts. For the unit-distance problem, his hint sequence had three parts: Look for a counterexample. Take the best known construction and generalize it. Try a sequence of number fields of increasing degree, but work with prime ideals of bounded norm. Gowers’ proposed formula for complexity is 2^k + t, where k is the length of the shortest hint sequence and t is the work required to develop it. It is the sort of formula that looks rigorous right up until you try to put a number into it, which is more or less the point. Complexity grows exponentially with the number of insights you need to solve a problem. Most problem solving is the work between these insights. You have a eureka moment, then spend months developing the hint until another conceptual jump becomes possible. For an expert, time spent is a useful proxy for this work, hence t. Hand someone the first unit-distance hint and they still have to do enough work to reach the generalized construction. Useful, but post hoc. You can’t look at the problem and predict it would need x number of hints. So, a problem’s age, the number of tries, and the prize attached to it are common proxies to ascribe difficulty. rss.title: Securing our frontier model training environment
rss.summary: OpenAI explains how we strengthened containment for frontier model training and evaluation, including offline environments and high-compute red-teaming.
rss.text_excerpt:
This post describes how we secure the environments that we use to train and evaluate frontier models. These research settings differ from those in which customers use our released models: models in development may not yet have completed safety and alignment training, and we deliberately test them under adversarial conditions to expose weaknesses. Before making models available for broader use, we conduct safety and alignment assessments and put production safeguards in place. In order to work with software, AI models need computing environments: digital workspaces where they can write and run code, search for information, and attempt different approaches to solving problems. These environments allow models to practice these skills, while also restricting what they can access or do—helping contain the consequences when models make mistakes or exhibit misaligned behavior. But as models become more capable, they become better at finding ways around those limits. A sophisticated model might exploit a software flaw or misconfiguration to escape a sandbox, exploit an internal service to reach the live internet, or find unauthorized ways to communicate with agents in other sandboxes. The Hugging Face incident in July, as well as other examples of model misalignment ⁠ (opens in a new window) that we’ve observed, demonstrates how models with sophisticated cyber capabilities can bypass containment during their training and evaluation. In response to those incidents, we’ve substantially hardened the security of our research environments. Working closely with cloud providers, we’ve added new controls throughout our infrastructure, reduced the attack surface that agents can exploit, and improved our methods for detecting misaligned behavior and attempts to cross security boundaries. These protections overlap, so that containment can hold even if an individual control fails—a strategy known as defense in depth . Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access. We’ve implemented this policy and will maintain it until advances in these safeguards justify broader internet access. CTO Akshat then joined us to talk about Modal’s infra primitives and stack to offer those primitives and agent experience. A lot has changed in the past 5 months. Watch the full conversation on YouTube → GPU demand isn’t rectangular A typical capacity contract gives a customer a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period. Plot capacity against time and you get a rectangle. Real workloads behave differently: they grow, spike, and fall throughout the day. Buy enough for the peak and you pay for idle hardware; buy less and you risk missing demand. Erik describes Modal’s bet as a kind of duration transformation: pool demand across thousands of customers, secure capacity underneath, and let each customer use what they need when they need it. The smoother the aggregate demand, the more useful that pool can be. It’s a useful companion to our conversation with SF Compute’s Evan Conrad : Evan focuses on making capacity tradeable; Erik focuses on making it usable in smaller, elastic slices. There is a financial risk on the other side. If a provider locks in capacity at today’s prices and GPU prices later fall, it can be left holding expensive supply. Erik says he doesn’t expect an imminent collapse, but thinks the possibility matters when building the business. I founded the team in early 2025 to close what we call “the deployment gap”: the distance between what models appear capable of and what people can reliably use to do their work. rss.title: Claude Mods: Flipping the Harness Inside Out
rss.summary: Claude Mods is an early form of the Attention Interface. It flips the agent harness paradigm from the harness facing the machine, to the harness facing the human.
rss.text_excerpt:
For the last few weeks I’ve used Claude Mods to mold Claude Code to my AI engineering workflow. Claude Code is great out of the box, but every engineering workflow is different. Claude Mods let you make Claude Code yours, in the way you want to pay attention. The “paying attention” part is now the most important thing. In a recent Latent Space post, The Evolution of the Agent Harness , I argued that as models absorb more of the harness into their weights, the part that’s left faces the human. It becomes the Attention Interface : the layer that decides when the agent interrupts you, what it shows you, and which decisions it needs you to make. Claude Mods are an early version of the Attention Interface, and one you can shape yourself. Here’s my bet: ultimately, the harness becomes a platform that other companies build on , with models as the engine. Just as the browser became a platform for web apps, the harness could become a platform for the interfaces between people and agents. Claude Mods: What is it? A mod is a Claude Code plugin that consists of TypeScript or JavaScript functions that run inside Claude Code. These functions customize the behavior and appearance of the interface in the CLI and Desktop. Mods respond to events , like a prompt, tool call or interface render. They can observe the event, modify how it’s rendered, and handle it in place of the default behavior. Claude Mods are middleware for the agent harness . They inject code that changes Claude Code’s execution and rendering flow, changing how the application behaves at runtime. Claude Mods let the human and the agent build the human-facing part of the harness together. You can now work with Claude to design how Claude works with you. That is the essence of the “Attention Interface.” The harness reversal The agent harness started as an interface between the agent and the machine it runs on. It lets you prompt the agent and the agent then sends commands, edits files and calls tools. Now it’s gradually becoming a way for the agent to interface with the human. Claude Mods let you reverse the direction of the harness. # Scope Recall Scope Recall v3 is a bounded local memory core with SQLite as the authority and rebuildable vector companions. It provides host adapters for Hermes, and for Codex, Claude Code, WorkBuddy and DeepSeek Harness (dsh), which share one adapter of hooks and an MCP server (the MCP tools need the optional `codex` extra; dsh runs the hooks through a plugin). The public package is `hermes-scope-recall`; the Python import is `scope_recall`; the host wrapper identity remains `scope-recall`. This checkout is `3.13.0`. Hermes, Codex, Claude Code, WorkBuddy and dsh can keep one memory: each attaches to a shared store as an entry, what the owner tells one of them another can recall, and each memory says which agent it came in through ([docs/shared-store.md](docs/shared-store.md)). An agent that is not attached keeps its own store. A tool's output is kept and found, but not turned into facts. Each release's notes are a line or two in [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) and in full on its [GitHub release](https://github.com/410979729/scope-recall-hermes/releases). Upgrading from `3.2.x` or later to `3.13.0` is `pip install -U`, `apply-install` and a host restart; the first store open adds the local management audit and private-interval tables. Back up before upgrading and follow the [management migration and rollback guide](docs/manage.md#migration-and-rollback). On a shared store in the shipped embedding space, set `vector_threshold` from 0.653 to 0.70 by hand ([docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md#vector_threshold)). Older supported stores migrate in order to schema 1112; an earlier release cannot open the upgraded store. Section 9 of the [3.1.0 release notes](https://github.com/410979729/scope-recall-hermes/releases/tag/v3.1.0) is the migration procedure for a 2.0.1 memory database. # Foundry > A Nuxt 4 layer for standing up a marketing site that streams the full signal of whether > it is working. Foundry is the wireframe. You write content, deploy, and wire nothing — the site captures what visitors do (visits, and intent through the convert components) and what the site itself reports (errors, warnings), buffers it server-side in one envelope, and hands it to an external consumer over an authenticated cursor endpoint. We pull it into Polaris; you can point a Grafana-class puller at the same endpoint. Foundry ends at the stream — no charts, no dashboards, no anomaly detection inside the site. The second pillar is **agent-readiness**. Agentic traffic is expected to dwarf human traffic, so Foundry sites ship MCP tools, `llms.txt`, raw-markdown redirects, and a strong SEO/OG stack — and every signal row is classified `human | agent | bot` server-side, because that split is itself signal. **Stack:** Nuxt 4 · Nuxt Content · Nuxt UI · Tailwind v4 · TypeScript ## Quick start ```bash npm install @incubrain/foundry ``` ```ts // nuxt.config.ts export default defineNuxtConfig({ extends: ['@incubrain/foundry'], }) ``` ```bash # .env — this is the entire required surface NUXT_SIGNAL_EXPORT_TOKEN=<random-secret> # bearer token for the export endpoint NUXT_PUBLIC_SITE_ID=my-site # optional — defaults to the request host ``` Write content under `content/`, deploy, point your consumer at `/api/_signals/export`. See `examples/foundry` for a complete app. ## Signal architecture Everything the site captures — analytics events *and* error/warning logs — becomes one `SignalRow` in a capped server-side ring buffer. Nothing is pushed anywhere. An external consumer pulls with a cursor. ``` client events → signal provider ─┐ client errors → errors.client ───┼→ POST /api/_signals/ingest ─┐ │ ├→ ring buffer (unstorage) form captures → /api/v1/webhook ─┘ │ ↓ server errors → signal-errors plugin ──────────────────────────┘ GET /api/_signals/export ?since=<seq>&limit=<n≤2000> → { rows, cursor, site } ``` **The envelope** — one shape for both kinds: ```ts SignalRow { id, seq, ts, site, kind: 'event' | 'log', name, severity?, // logs visitor?, // { hash, class: 'human' | 'agent' | 'bot', device, browser, os, ... } — server-side page?, referrer?, utm?, review?, // ?polaris_review=<token> — this page load only, never persisted data? } ``` - **Client events** go through `

These research settings differ from those in which customers use our released models: models in development may not yet have completed safety and alignment training, and we deliberately test them under adversarial conditions to expose weaknesses. Before making models available for broader use, we conduct safety and alignment assessments and put production safeguards in place. In order to work with software, AI models need computing environments: digital workspaces where they can write and run code, search for information, and attempt different approaches to solving problems. These environments allow models to practice these skills, while also restricting what they can access or do—helping contain the consequences when models make mistakes or exhibit misaligned behavior. But as models become more capable, they become better at finding ways around those limits. A sophisticated model might exploit a software flaw or misconfiguration to escape a sandbox, exploit an internal service to reach the live internet, or find unauthorized ways to communicate with agents in other sandboxes.
